extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and writers interested in gothic/psychological horror novels
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points relevant to creating or analyzing a haunted-house gothic / psychological-horror novel, focusing on Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House as an exemplar. Emphasizes research, setting, perspective, ambiguity, and thematic subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and use of source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Jackson researched nineteenth-century 'psychic researchers' and read many traditional ghost stories; she claimed to have found a magazine picture of a suitably haunted-looking house and used it as inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical or documentary sources (reports, magazine images, traditional stories) as raw material; mining 'dry reports' can reveal human motivations and conflicts to dramatize rather than simply copying supernatural claims. Example: Jackson's reading of psychic reports led her to focus on the earnest people involved rather than sensational supernatural claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance on reality/ghosts (decide belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jackson wrote: 'No one can get into a novel about a haunted house without hitting the subject of reality head-on; either I have to believe in ghosts, which I do, or I have to write another kind of novel altogether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early whether the narrative treats ghosts as literal or as psychological/metaphorical; this choice should shape tone and structure. Being explicit about the author's approach (or deliberately equivocal) influences whether the book reads as supernatural horror or psychological study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial planning and concrete setting design
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of her process, Jackson sketched floor plans of the downstairs and upstairs of Hill House and a rendering of the exterior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the physical space (floor plans, exterior renderings) to ensure spatial consistency and to enable setting-driven plot moments (doors, stairs, blind spots). Detailed spatial planning can make uncanny occurrences feel grounded and plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity in supernatural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the supernatural phenomena are described only vaguely, or are partly hidden from the characters themselves; at least some of what Eleanor witnesses may be a product of her imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor suggestive, vague depiction of strange events rather than explicit explanation. Ambiguity sustains tension and invites multiple interpretations, allowing the uncanny to persist beyond the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven horror (focus on inner lives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argued the horror in the novel 'does not lie in Hill House... but in the unexplored recesses of its characters' – and its readers' – minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize psychological depth and the characters' interiority over external shocks. Let interpersonal dynamics, desires, fears, and memory produce the novel's dread rather than relying solely on visible supernatural spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of limited/unreliable perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleanor tends to experience phenomena to which the others are oblivious; some of the disturbances may be products of her imagination or subconscious abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a focalized or unreliable viewpoint (one character's perception) to create doubt about what's 'really' happening. Contrast that perspective with other characters' experiences to heighten uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse, intensely written scenes over constant action
rubrics_metrics.description: Carmen Maria Machado: 'Even though the events that appear to be supernatural activity are few and far between, those scenes are so chillingly written...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on a few well-crafted, chilling scenes rather than continuous or gratuitous horror. Precision and intensity in select moments produce greater lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present multiple plausible explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel suggests possibilities such as Eleanor's imagination or a subconscious telekinetic ability as causes for disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple interpretive avenues (psychological, supernatural, physiological) so readers can inhabit different explanatory frameworks. Avoid forcing a single definitive answer unless intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate the setting's dark history into atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Montague explains the building's history, which encompasses suicide and other violent deaths, and this history is used to build dread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave backstory (deaths, past events) into the present atmosphere; historical details about a house or place can justify mood and suggest latent forces without explicit manifestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast through secondary characters' non-experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Some visitors (Mrs. Montague and Arthur Parker) do not experience supernatural events, though alleged spirit writings seem to communicate with Eleanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters who do not perceive the uncanny as foils to the focal character's experiences; these contrasts can underline the protagonist's isolation and unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversion of genre tropes and thematic layering
rubrics_metrics.description: Joanne Harris described the book as 'not only the best haunted-house story ever written, but also a quiet subversion of the ingénue trope in horror fiction...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally subvert common genre expectations (e.g., ingénue tropes) to add complexity and thematic depth. Layer references (philosophical or literary allusions) to enrich interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation choices that grant agency (queer characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sara Century pointed out queer themes, noting Theodora 'stands out for being an imperfect, fallible queer woman... still walking away from [danger], evolving rather than fading away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray marginalized characters (e.g., queer characters) with complexity and agency rather than as disposable tropes. Avoid cliché outcomes like 'bury your gays' by granting narrative development and survival where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of explanation—let fear arise from suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The text often leaves phenomena unexplained and relies on suggestion and implication to create terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist over-explaining the source of horror; allowance for the unknown amplifies dread. Use implication, partial revelations, and withheld information as a craft technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability: retain core elements when translating media
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptations vary in faithfulness: the 1963 film is relatively faithful and praised; the 1999 version diverged and was widely panned; the 2018 Netflix series kept setting and a few names but shifted focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting the material to other media, identify and preserve the novel's core elements (tone, central themes, key setting motifs) while acknowledging that medium changes may require shifts in focus. Faithfulness to psychological subtlety is often critical to reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical measures of success: subtlety and skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary and later critics praise Jackson for being 'the finest master' of the haunted tale and for treating potentially pulpy material 'with great skill and subtlety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or write with attention to craft: subtle handling of grim or sensational subject matter, restraint, and skilled prose often distinguish enduring works in the genre.
